items.question: Why do you see human task duration as a useful metric for tracking AI progress over many years?
items.object: METR’s use of human task duration to measure AI progress
items.answer:
Basically, the typical way we measure progress in AI is via benchmarks. A benchmark is a set of tasks that you have an AI system, this could be a neural network or an agent or whatever, try and complete. You count up how many of the tasks the model succeeded at. When you create the benchmark, typically models do very poorly, and then over time people iterate and you can track progress on the benchmark. Eventually AI developers will achieve saturation, so model performance will either reach 100% or there'll be some errors in the benchmark and the model will do as well as it can reasonably be expected to do, because we think about there being a noise ceiling on some benchmarks.

It's difficult with normal benchmarks to track progress over a very long period of time, because benchmarks are typically restricted to some particular domain or the tasks have a somewhat similar level of difficulty. To try and understand how progress in AI happens over many years, before this work the status quo was comparing different benchmarks to one another. It's 2017 and you have simple problems for models, and they can start doing those; now it's 2025 and we have way harder benchmarks, and we can see there's been a lot of progress. But it's really hard; we don't actually have a single metric to track this progress.

We're kind of doing this qualitative comparison of the difficulty of benchmarks over time, and this is messy and people have different priors. This work was motivated by trying to have a y-axis, basically a way of tracking progress and seeing what the trends in AI progress have been over a longer period of time than individual benchmarks typically have. The way we operationalize this is we look at the length of tasks, the length of task for humans that models are 50% likely, or some percent likely, to be able to succeed at. We have a really wide range of tasks, ranging from a few seconds all the way up to eight or 10 hours. Crucially, this is the time the tasks take for people to complete.

items.question: What do you find significant about measuring AI progress by the length of tasks models can complete?
items.object: METR’s task-duration metric for measuring AI progress
items.answer:
We have a combination of having a bunch of people attempt the tasks and seeing how long they take, as well as just estimating how long the tasks take. For any individual model, we see that models do really well on the very short tasks and then much more poorly on the long tasks. We look at, for some given success likelihood, how long are those tasks, and we estimate this in a particular way that we could get into. The main takeaway is we want to see, for different models, how long are the tasks they can complete. The striking thing that we found is that over the past roughly five years there's been an extremely robust, systematic trend in the length of tasks that models are able to complete.

To our best ability to understand the data that we're seeing, it seems like this is fit very well by an exponential function. The length of tasks that models are able to complete has been increasing exponentially over this period. There are big questions over how well we can expect this to continue in the future, but over this period, at least with this data that we've collected, there's been this exponential trend. That's the striking result, and the key novelty for us is this unified metric that can be applied to different benchmarks. For different benchmarks, you can measure how long these tasks take people, right? For very simple natural language processing benchmarks that were common in the 2010s, these tasks typically don't take people very long, like a few seconds.

A lot of the tasks that people are having agents complete now, like difficult software engineering tasks, take people somewhere in the range of hours or something, and models can sometimes complete those, although they're still somewhat unreliable.

items.question: How do you think METR should choose the people whose task completion times define its AI time horizon metric?
items.object: Human expertise sampling for METR’s time horizon metric
items.answer: I think there are different reasonable ways of doing this. You could randomly sample a person in the world, off the street or something, to do each task. I think this wouldn't be a very useful measure of how long these tasks take people, because in general those people are not completing these tasks in the real world. The thing we're trying to get at with this metric is, we want it to be very intuitive. We want it to be clear: if an AI system can do tasks of length 15, 30 minutes, an hour, two hours, how does that translate into the real world? We want that connection to be very direct, and so we want to have people attempt these tasks that we would naturally expect to be doing these tasks in the world. We try and have people who have a reasonable amount of expertise in the different areas, who we might expect to do them. That's the expertise sampling question.

items.question: How do you think human attempts should be used to estimate task completion times for METR's time-horizon metric?
items.object: Estimating human task completion times for METR's time-horizon metric
items.answer: Sometimes they succeed and sometimes they fail. There's this question of, do we include their failures? Do we just use successful times? I think there's reasonable discussion about this. One thing it would be nice to do is include their failures. If we have someone who has a reasonable amount of expertise but they fail at a task, I think that is information about the task being more difficult. But you would need a larger number of people to attempt the tasks in order to actually use that information. You could do something like survival analysis from the medical industry, where you know that they failed after a certain amount of time, but it's possible that they would have succeeded in the future. Anyways, what we actually do in the paper is we use the geometric mean of the successful attempts. We use the geometric mean because we think completion time broadly is distributed logarithmically, or sometimes people will take much longer than other people, and we don't want that to totally dominate the time we're estimating for the tasks.

items.question: What do you see as the distinctive value of the time horizon metric for measuring AI capabilities?
items.object: The time horizon metric for measuring AI capabilities
items.answer:
In terms of the unique value of this approach that we're taking with this time horizon metric, there are a lot of benchmarks that try and come up with the most difficult questions for people and then have AI try and do them. This is in fact the standard methodology for saying, “This AI system is smarter than another one”: it can do problems that fewer and fewer people can do. We started out with common sense questions that most people can do in the 2010s; over the past couple years models have been able to do them. I worked on this benchmark GPQA that had very difficult science questions, roughly PhD level. Models are able to do that now, and GPQA I think is mostly saturated or pretty close to it.

Models can do IMO questions, International Math Olympiad questions, that very few people can do. I think this is an important axis to measure AI capabilities along: difficulty for people. But I think this misses a lot of what people can do that AI systems can't do. One of the key things we're trying to get at is how can we reconcile the fact that models can do these IMO questions, that they're geniuses in some sense, but they're kind of idiots still?

You ask it to book a flight for you—and maybe models can do that now—but even slightly harder things, they kind of fall over often. I think that's the thing we're trying to get at. We want to factor out how much expertise do you need. One intuition for what we're trying to get at is something like the number of actions that are required to complete this task. I think this is very difficult to operationalize, or problematic and mushy. But one intuition is that if we factor out the difficulty of problems and just look at how long they take people who have a reasonable amount of expertise, maybe we're getting closer to something like agency more broadly.

I don't want to overclaim. I think this is still very much an open area, but, for example, number of actions is also a very reasonable thing that I would expect to be correlated, although it's probably more difficult to estimate.

items.question: How do you think about what makes the hardest tasks in your evaluations difficult?
items.object: The difficulty of the hardest tasks in METR's evaluations
items.answer:
The hardest tasks we have take people six, seven, 10 hours to complete. One of the sets of tasks we use comes from this benchmark that we released about a year ago, or close to a year ago, called RE-Bench, which stands for Research Engineering Bench. This is a set of challenging ML research engineering tasks. One example is you're given a neural network whose embeddings are permuted in a way that you don't know; they're scrambled, and your task is to fix the embeddings of this model. You can do fine-tuning or data analysis to try and understand how they were scrambled and see if you can reconstruct them.

It requires intuitions about how neural networks work and how to fine-tune or work with models at a relatively low level. There are a range of other tasks, but these tasks take ML engineers roughly eight hours to do decently well on. That's one class of tasks. We have other kinds of software engineering tasks, for example, or cybersecurity tasks that take quite a bit of time. One example—I think we didn't actually get a baseline on this; we're just estimating how long it takes—is a task with a modified implementation of an older standard hashing algorithm, MD5, and the task is to find a hash collision on this modified version of this older hashing algorithm. There are standard attacks that work on this algorithm.

There's literature on attacks. It's not impervious, but you have to know which are the right ones. You have to understand the algorithm pretty well, and then you have to be able to modify the attacks or figure out how to change it. This one is a little bit more expertise-heavy, maybe, than serial-action-heavy, and so there's a bit of range there.

items.question: Why do you think METR should focus on measuring AI capabilities in domains like software engineering, cybersecurity, and AI R&D?
items.object: METR's focus on measuring AI capabilities in software engineering, cybersecurity, and AI R&D
items.answer:
I think there are at least a few reasons. One reason is that some of the threat models that METR is most concerned about are contingent on AI capabilities in some of these particular domains, like software engineering, cybersecurity, and AI R&D in particular. We're most interested in measurements of AI capabilities in these domains because we think these are highly relevant for estimating risk, in particular catastrophic risk from AI systems.

That's one reason: they're just directly relevant. Another reason is there has been a lot more focus from AI developers on these domains, and so we're measuring something that's closer to what they're focused on. I think this has some trade-offs. One objection is, “AI systems are really bad at other stuff because developers aren't focused on it, and so now you're overestimating their capabilities.” I think that's a legitimate concern, or I think that is true. But there's this question of whether the methods that AI developers are applying to improve models in these particular domains are general enough and are working well in these domains. If they're general, we might expect it to be relatively easy, or more a product of general commercialization, to apply these methods now to a broader range of tasks.

I think there's this idea that we want to aim for some balance of these, and we want to understand how much generalization there can be from these domains. There are open questions around this, but I think that's another reason. Finally, it's just easier to measure AI capabilities in these domains. We're software engineers. In particular, one big thing is if you want to have a benchmark that's easy to run and easy to evaluate a model's performance on, it's much easier to do this in domains where you can more formally verify model outputs. If you want to understand how well models can summarize text or write creative fiction, it's really hard to write some code or automatically verify that this creative fiction is actually good. There are ways of getting around this to some extent.

items.question: How do you assess human difficulty ratings and human success probabilities as alternative measures of AI task difficulty?
items.object: Human difficulty ratings and human success probabilities as measures of AI task difficulty

items.question: Why do you filter your human task baselines to successful attempts when measuring AI time horizons?
items.object: Filtering human task baselines to successful attempts
items.answer: One of the reasons why we filter our baselines to only ones that succeed is success on a task is a lot more information than failure on a task. There are a bunch of reasons why you might fail a task that aren't actually a lot of information about how difficult it is or how much agency is required. For example, maybe we got their expertise wrong. We're doing this job of manually assigning people to tasks that we think they're relevant for, or that they have a lot of relevant expertise for, and maybe someone just happened to never use this particular tool or set of tools that are super important for this task. Then their failure on that task is still some information, but if they succeed on the task, then that is this very objective thing: yes, someone can complete this task in this amount of time. There are also infrastructure reasons why people fail tasks, and incentive reasons. When you have people try and complete tasks, sometimes they'll get bored and want to stop; sometimes they'll be like, “Ah, this is too hard. I don't want to keep doing this.” Sometimes incentives can be tricky to set up well. One situation you can have is where people quit tasks early because they want to maximize the chances of getting more tasks that they succeed on. Typically we pay bonuses for success because we want to incentivize people to succeed, but that can lead to a perverse incentive. Broadly, we just have a lot more uncertainty about failures than we do about successes.

items.question: How do you view task messiness as a way to explain AI systems' successes and failures?

items.answer:

The length of task for humans is one metric that explains a decent amount of this variance, but there are definitely other things going on. We're actually currently trying to figure out what other properties of tasks explain their success and failure well. We would love to have something like this. For something like messiness, or a lot of these other kinds of metrics you can think of, to me the biggest issue or challenge is just some kind of subjectivity. People have very different senses of what is a messy versus clean task.

One example is I have a colleague who would not rate any of our tasks as being messy at all because they have algorithmic scoring functions, for example. The success or failure is defined by a small surface area or something. items.question: How do you interpret the apparent acceleration in METR’s measured AI task time horizons after 2024?
items.object: Whether METR’s measured AI task time horizons are improving super-exponentially
items.answer:
I think we still don't really know. A couple things to say: one thing it'd be useful to point out for listeners is that this plot where we measure the trend of improvement over time is only using the best model at a given time. That's relevant because a lot of other models have different trade-offs; maybe they have faster inference but they're weaker, and we're just using the models that perform the best.

I think the timeline is useful for understanding how the paper came together: we initially only fit the trend on models from, I think, basically 2024 onwards. The first version of the graph was made by Ben West in December 2024, if my memory is right, and I think this was just using that year's models. With those models, we observed this four-month doubling time in the time horizon. Then we were like, does this trend extend backwards? In the paper we also do these backcasts from this. Then we added in previous models.

All that's to say that to some extent from the start we've seen these two trends. I think this is all kind of BS or something; once you have 10 or 15 data points and you're fitting piecewise linear functions, it's pretty sketchy. I definitely don't want to overclaim, but it does seem like this four-month doubling-time trend from 2024 onwards has continued to hold, or has been a much better predictor than the seven-month doubling time suggested by models going back to 2019. My best guess, with very low confidence, is something like we're just on this four-month trend now, but it's still exponential. It is really hard to distinguish between different kinds of model fits to some extent.

items.question: How do you assess the cost competitiveness of AI agents on longer tasks?
items.object: The cost competitiveness of AI agents on longer tasks
items.answer: You can do much better with caching. Most APIs let you do prefix caching, and that helps quite a bit, so you should count it kind of differently, I think. But it's a big chunk. Models will do lots of reasoning and run a bunch of different experiments on these longer tasks. They'll take something like 10 to 50 actions in the environment, but for each action they're doing a bunch of reasoning. Often, depending on the exact agent scaffold, we have models that propose actions and then review them and select the best one. There's a lot going on, and this is still much cheaper than having people do it. I wish I knew the exact numbers on cost. It is more complicated because of caching, but currently this isn't our biggest concern because models are still highly cost-competitive. I totally imagine this changing at some point. Trends in models being able to use test-time compute more effectively—I totally expect for very long tasks this to get expensive, and it to be very important to be measuring the Pareto frontier of cost and success rate. I think we're excited to do work on this as it becomes more relevant.

items.question: Why do you see measuring AI systems’ software engineering and ML research capabilities as important to METR’s work on AI risk?
items.object: METR’s focus on measuring AI software engineering and ML research capabilities
items.answer:
The threat model that METR is most concerned about, at least at the moment, is rapid acceleration in AI capabilities, and in fact the rate of progress of AI capabilities, due to AI systems being able to contribute substantially, or the majority of AI progress, at some point in the future. Currently the way you make AI systems better is through a combination of compute, hardware resources, money, data, and talent, labor, right? If it becomes the case that AI systems can replace the labor, the talent part of this, in economic models of progress—in at least some of them, I think they're reasonable, although I'm not an economist—you can see very rapid progress. This just seems broadly scary.

One example is very rapid centralization of power in a single organization that does this kind of recursive self-improvement, and that's concerning for general stability, geopolitical, democracy kinds of reasons. And then your arguments for why the AI system itself is not going to be dangerous might break down. You might not be able to evaluate it effectively, because the system may have a really good understanding of exactly how you're evaluating it. If its goals are different from yours, it might be very easy for it to game your evaluations. Your supervision methods might break down. You're reading its chains of thought, and the model is saying things that seem safe and nice and reasonable, but actually it's doing some hidden reasoning in the background that you can't detect.

You didn't realize this was about to happen because progress was so fast, and because as a lab you were scrambling to get as much compute and make as much progress as you can as quickly as you can. Broadly, one of the big concerns or questions we want to understand is how close are we to this rapid acceleration? Is that even possible? Labor is not the only input to AI progress. You also have compute and data, for example. These things might be highly complementary to labor, such that even if the amount of talent increases by several orders of magnitude because you have all your AI researchers doing this work, you still might be bottlenecked by compute and data. Trying to get some understanding of that, we do some work or think about these economic models to some extent. I think this isn't our chief forte. Epoch has a bunch of great work doing some of this modeling. Folks at Forethought, Will MacAskill and Tom Davidson, have done work on this kind of economic modeling. Understanding how capable AI systems are is a big input to this, and software engineering and ML research capabilities are highly relevant.

The actual inputs to this progress are firms competing to train increasingly better models and putting these resources in, and they have constraints and whatever. I think this was one of the big updates for me. items.question: How do you think AI time horizons can help identify when AI systems will substantially accelerate AI progress?
items.object: Using AI time horizons to anticipate AI accelerating AI progress
items.answer:
I think this is an open question. I don't think we have nearly as good an answer here yet as we want. We have heuristics, I think. One week of work, like time horizons of 40 hours: I think we're definitely getting a lot more concerned, or it seems at least plausible that you could successfully or efficiently delegate weeks' worth of work to AI systems, and I could totally imagine that speeding up AI progress quite a bit. Same for time horizons that are much longer, but I think we don't really know.

Part of my uncertainty—I probably would have been more confident in something like a week or a few weeks of work as a time horizon that's very useful as some rough heuristic or threshold before this productivity RCT, where we found that people were very miscalibrated on how much AI systems sped them up, developers, software developers in particular, and in fact we saw they were slowed down on average by about 20%. I think the time horizons work and the randomized control trial results probably aren't as in conflict as they might seem at face value, for reasons we could talk about. They definitely did update me more towards broader uncertainty about this interaction between AI systems and people, and maybe we do end up really bottlenecked by things like our ability to specify tasks really clearly, or maybe things like the fact that we're algorithmically scoring models mean we might be overestimating their capabilities to some extent.

items.question: How do you think about the trade-off between granular skill benchmarks and realistic tasks when evaluating AI systems?
items.object: Granular versus realistic benchmarks for evaluating AI systems
items.answer:
I think there is a very real trade-off here between the level of granularity of your understanding—if you maximize that, you end up with very simple, formulaic, systematic benchmarks that are probing some particular skill—and on the other end you have this realism-maximization lens. The best popular example of this maybe is SWE-bench or SWE-bench Verified, where these are actual GitHub issues and PRs and tests that you're measuring AI systems against. There's a real trade-off: on one end you get this granular understanding, and on the other it's really easy to interpret what a success or failure means. It's like, yes, it can do this thing in the real world that I understand and have intuitions about. I think there's a real trade-off.

What do I think here? I think it's really hard. Broadly, I feel pretty pessimistic about the granular approach. Maybe this has something to do with the amount of systematicity in neural networks themselves, where they're just inconsistent but are still capable of really impressive things. Maybe you can't get this extremely crisp understanding and you have to aggregate or look more broadly at things that are relevant for your decisions about whether to deploy a system or how safe it is. That's probably the direction I lean in.

items.question: What do you see as the main challenges in extending METR’s time-horizon evaluations to longer tasks?
items.object: Extending METR’s time-horizon evaluation methodology to longer tasks
items.answer:
Broadly, there are a few things. One is continuing to use this methodology. Currently models have 50% success rates on these two-hour tasks. GPT-5, I think, is two hours and 15 minutes or something. If we really are on this four-month doubling-time trend, that's four hours by the end of the year, eight hours in spring of next year, 16 hours in fall next year. That's not that long. We have fewer longer tasks and fewer baselines on these longer tasks because they're more difficult to baseline: you have to find people with more specialized expertise, they're more expensive, and people fail more often.

Extending our task suite and trying to see, does this trend continue, is one big direction. There are open questions around how do we affordably continue doing this? Are we harvesting tasks from existing work that people have already done, or creating new tasks and using LLM evaluation or more manual review to evaluate success? Are we doing other things? That's one class of things: trying to continue this basic methodology.

items.question: How do you think about whether benchmarks such as SWE-bench accurately measure model success?
items.object: SWE-bench and the validity of AI benchmark scores
items.answer:
I think there's another class of directions we're pretty excited about, which is something more like—we have benchmark development and evaluating models on these tasks, but then there are questions around how good are our benchmarks and how good are other benchmarks. Over the last couple weeks I've been labeling many dozens of attempts of models on SWE-bench with a bunch of different factors to try and understand, for example, how good are our tests in SWE-bench? Are models often implementing correct functionality that isn't captured by the tests because the tests were written for the specific implementation that the human originally wrote? Alternatively, are models often succeeding as judged by the automatic test cases, but they're actually breaking a bunch of other code that isn't tested in the repo, or their solution is just bad in some other ways so we wouldn't actually call that a success?

Broadly, this is one example of this stream of work we've started doing more of over the past few months: trying to understand benchmarks, the science of evals. How can we interpret certain scores on different benchmarks, ones we've made and ones other folks have made?

items.question: What open questions do you see about the future usefulness of METR’s capability evaluations for estimating AI risk?
items.object: The future usefulness of METR’s capability evaluations for estimating AI risk
items.answer: Broadly, we've covered a fair bit of METR's capability evaluation work. There are big open questions to me around how long we'll be able to continue doing this work—not even just from a tractability perspective, but also from a “will it actually be useful?” perspective, in particular for estimating risk. items.question: How did the problem of scalable oversight shape your thinking about AI evaluations and motivate GPQA?
items.object: Scalable oversight and the motivation for GPQA
items.answer: For me, it was mostly thinking about this problem of scalable oversight. As models get more capable, it just gets harder to evaluate their capabilities. If we imagine that models are able to complete tasks that take people a long time to complete or require expertise that you don't necessarily have, you need a method for still being confident in their outputs and trusting their outputs. And so thinking about that problem was a lot of motivation actually for GPQA, and was what kind of started, got me started thinking about evaluations.

items.question: Why do you use human completion time as a unified measure of AI progress?
items.object: Human completion time as a unified measure of AI progress
items.answer:
I guess the place to start for us in terms of the motivation for the time horizon work is to have a unified axis that we can measure AI progress on over a very long period of time. So when we started doing the work, we had this very strong belief that GPT-2 is fundamentally, in some really important sense, much worse as an AI than, I guess, at the time it was maybe Sonnet 3.5, I think, the best model out then. The standard approach is producing, creating a set of tasks and then measuring models' accuracy on these tasks. As models get better, they saturate the benchmark. And then you have to create a new benchmark that has harder tasks. This was kind of the standard approach. And I contributed a benchmark, GPQA, to this approach. But the challenge here is that it's really difficult to compare between these qualitatively different benchmarks. So the set of tasks you evaluate GPT-2 on are like LAMBADA, like complete the last word in this text. And tasks that we were having Sonnet 3.5 try and do were kind of like answer simple Python coding questions, or write a short 20-line Python program. And so it's very difficult, at first blush, to say, okay, yeah, how much harder is writing a Python program than finishing the word in this paragraph? It's kind of hard to think about that.

And so I think the key insight of the time horizons work is to use this notion of human time to complete. So how long does the task take a human to do? A human who has a reasonable amount of expertise such that they would plausibly be doing the task in their work or in their day to day. And the idea was we can use this metric to represent the difficulty of the task in some sense. And then we can compare models across a very wide range of capabilities, all the way from GPT-2 now up to Opus 4.6. That's the high level motivation.

items.question: How do you design time horizon benchmark tasks to probe models' ability to generalize beyond their training data?
items.object: Designing time horizon benchmark tasks to test generalization
items.answer:
On the longer end, we have tasks that either require quite a bit of expertise or many steps to complete. So we have machine learning tasks that are train a model in this kind of—that's very weird, such that the code for training this model is not really online. One example is train a masked language model without using the division or exponentiation operators. And so you actually have to be pretty clever about how you set up the architecture to do this. And the hope is that this can help us measure models' ability to generalize beyond their training data.

There are some which are a bit like ARC-AGI, sort of the themed in that they're like, you have some black box that's computing some function, and you know that it's a composition of some set of primitives, and you've gotta figure out what function it is. Or you have some long binary string, and you've gotta figure out what the pattern continuation is, and sort of puzzle type tasks where it's very—you know, some ML type tasks can be basically regurgitating a tutorial on how to build your first ResNet or whatever, just works pretty well. So, yeah, having these weird tasks that are either some kind of unknown object that you need to interact with and figure out what it is, or a task that resembles normal work but has some weird constraints such that you can't just do the standard thing. I don't think all of our tasks hit those criteria. Some of them, you can just do the standard thing, but we generally try to avoid that.
